title: There’s No Such Thing as an AI ‘Lab’
excerpt: When did AI companies become AI labs ? That term, and the image of studious, exacting white-coated scientists that it conjures, has become curiously entrenched
body: When did AI companies become AI labs ? That term, and the image of studious, exacting white-coated scientists that it conjures, has become curiously entrenched as a descriptor for the businesses swiftly escorting the world into an existentially unsettling future

AI companies themselves have embraced the label: When Chris Olah, a co-founder of Anthropic, addressed the pope earlier this year, he repeatedly referred to his company, one of the most powerful AI enterprises in the world, as a lab
Industry press releases, technology commentators, and news publications have all picked up the word too
You’ll see the term on transit advertisements in San Francisco and in the pages of The New York Times (and, yes, The Atlantic )
Here is my proposal: Everyone, please stop

Although AI companies do invest heavily in research and development, using a word typically associated with groups of truth-seeking scientists is misleading, odd, and too favorable to these companies’ own ends
As a software engineer working in tech, I’ve seen little evidence that AI companies’ research practices differ significantly from those of the rest of the tech industry
Google and Microsoft, for example, have robust research divisions, but we still call them companies
So why has the laboratory term become so deeply enmeshed with AI? Part of the reason is historical
Over the past century, research laboratories have played a crucial role in computer science
Studies performed at Bell Labs, one of America’s first industrial labs, resulted in the development of the transistor and the cellular network
In the 1970s, scientists at the MIT Laboratory for Computer Science pioneered the foundations of modern cryptography

As the Harvard historian Steven Shapin writes in his book The Scientific Life , countless innovations such as these that originated in corporate labs during the 20th century helped change the public’s perception of science
No longer simply knowledge for knowledge’s sake, science became viewed as a key engine of societal and economic progress
In their early years, OpenAI and Anthropic mainly performed research, similar to other industrial labs
Since then, however, they have commercialized rapidly: Each company is now valued near $1 trillion and generates billions in quarterly revenue
Holding on to the lab label seems to have the obvious PR benefit of allowing both companies to lean into their scientific legacy
Because of concerns about child safety, privacy, and job displacement, Americans largely hold a negative perception of the industry—and tech as a whole

That’s translated into popular opposition from politicians, data-center activists, and religious leaders who are concerned about the outsize influence of these companies: Spending on AI as a share of U.S
Meanwhile, scientists remain relatively popular
A 2026 Pew Research Center poll found that more than 75 percent of Americans trust scientists to act in the public interest, but the majority do not trust business leaders to do the same
These positive connotations associated with scientific research help the AI industry signal altruism while downplaying their profit-making ambitions
OpenAI and Anthropic’s leaders write at length about how AI’s risks and perils must be carefully studied for the sake of humanity
Research is portrayed as essential to this mission: OpenAI says it treats “ safety as a science ,” and Anthropic writes that “providing trustworthy research” will improve policy outcomes
The problem is, these companies act much more like private enterprises than bastions of science
Much of the research listed in the Publications section on both Anthropic’s and OpenAI’s websites are not peer-reviewed papers accepted by scholarly outlets
I examined 100 recent pieces of research from both companies’ Research pages; the overwhelming majority had no corresponding peer-reviewed paper accepted by a conference or journal

It’s unclear whether these were submitted to academic venues and, if so, whether they were rejected, are under review, or are forthcoming. (Neither OpenAI nor Anthropic responded to requests for comment.) Legal risks and long peer-review cycles are typically cited as reasons that fast-moving tech companies seldom share data or engage in peer review
And to its credit, the industry doesn’t always choose research topics that paint its products in a positive light
Anthropic has conducted studies on its models’ undesirable behaviors, such as disempowerment and sycophancy
Even so, Anthropic has a habit of landing on ambiguity about the fallout of its technology

In its education report , for instance, Anthropic, the entity best equipped to observe whether students are using Claude to cheat, concludes that the question of “How much are students using AI to cheat?” is “hard to answer.” The practice of assuming scientific authority while exercising potentially biased research practices has more in common with quasi-scientific advocacy organizations than it does with traditional laboratories
Marshall Institute, a think tank founded in 1984 whose leaders worked closely with the Reagan White House

The institute, whose publications defended oil interests and the tobacco industry, operated under the motto “Science for better public policy.” As the historians Naomi Oreskes and Erik Conway reported in the book Merchants of Doubt , the institute strategically refused to publish in journals subject to independent peer review

Instead, it disseminated reports and briefings to policy makers that merely reproduced the “trappings of scientific argumentation—graphs, charts, references, and the like.” If Anthropic, OpenAI, and other AI giants want to keep referring to themselves as labs, they should adhere to scientific best practices: open-sourcing code, preregistering studies, and, most important, subjecting research to independent peer review
Ultimately, AI companies such as Anthropic and OpenAI aren’t tweedy labs doing arcane research—they’re industry-defining corporations reshaping our workplaces, our schools, and our communities
Holding them accountable could start with calling them out for what they are—and what they aren’t.

title: What Tech Titans Don’t Understand About Sci-Fi
excerpt: This is an edition of the Books Briefing, our editors’ weekly guide to the best in books
body: This is an edition of the Books Briefing, our editors’ weekly guide to the best in books

When I read Thomas More’s Utopia in college, the main thing I retained was that the inhabitants of More’s imaginary island worked just six hours a day and earned what we might now call a universal basic income

But the fact that I came away from this 16th-century classic with only visions of a shorter workday and a generous allowance says more about my undergraduate habits than it does about More’s ideas or intentions
Looking back recently, I remembered that his civilization wasn’t exactly the campus commune of my dreams
Its citizens held slaves, some of whom were shackled for committing adultery
The punishment for premarital sex, meanwhile, was permanent celibacy; the whole place sounded like a punitive surveillance state
Still, as Gal Beckerman noted this week in an Atlantic essay about Silicon Valley’s misreadings of science fiction , I wasn’t the first person to make this type of error

First, here are five new stories from The Atlantic Books Section: The sexual politics of the “bed trick” What Howard Zinn got wrong “Red Death,” a poem by Dorothea Lasky What to read to wake up your brain Roy Cohn did it first
In her new book, The Rise and Fall of the Artificial State , the historian Jill Lepore close-reads the science-fiction books that proved formative for Elon Musk, Sam Altman, and Peter Thiel
In their early-teen years, these future billionaires devoured the works of Robert Heinlein, Isaac Asimov, Arthur C
Clarke, and other dark fantasists—but they seem to still hold on to the blinkered interpretations from their youth

Their collective misunderstandings fascinated Beckerman. “What they seemed not to get,” he writes of these men, “was that these were cautionary tales, stories that projected deep societal worries into space or onto a future many millennia away.” Instead of seeing the dysfunction behind these invented societies, “these boys just thought the killer robots sounded cool.” Lepore argues that these seeming misreads are partly responsible for their obsessions with technological progress—no matter the human cost

Three centuries after More coined the word utopia (which sounds in Greek like “good place” but actually means “no place”), the philosopher John Stuart Mill effectively popularized its opposite, dystopia , to describe worlds in which the worst things come to pass
In the 20th century, dystopia became a key feature of science fiction
Some of my favorite works in the genre introduce us to societies that seem idyllic, before revealing the rot within these supposedly perfect worlds
They aim, I think, to show that any utopia is probably too good to be true
More’s Utopia isn’t all that different; it depicts a society that readers might not actually want to live in
More, an English Catholic leader who was executed by King Henry VIII, probably didn’t mean to advocate for an essentially communist society with legalized euthanasia
Critics have long speculated that his depiction was satirical—that the first utopian literary work was, at least in part, dystopian
This wouldn’t surprise me, because years of living and reading have conditioned me to accept that every paradise has a dark side

This is why I was dismayed to hear Sam Altman say, earlier this year, that an AI-driven process to choose the U.S. president could be “awesome.” Seventy years ago, in his short story “Franchise,” Asimov imagined one variation on this scenario: A computer picks one median American to “vote” for president
In the story, democracy becomes nothing more than a statistical quirk

At a moment when artificial intelligence threatens to change society irrevocably, I have to agree with Beckerman: “What happens next,” he writes, “may depend on whether these boys grow up and finally recognize what they failed to see before.” Illustration by Matteo Giuseppe Pani / The Atlantic * We Are Living in the Fantasy World of 13-Year-Old Boys By Gal Beckerman Many of the tech billionaires who built our world have taken the wrong lessons from their favorite science fiction
What to Read Providence , by Max Barry Seven years before the start of this novel, an alien species slaughtered everyone aboard a human spaceship—Earth’s first contact with extraterrestrials
Providence follows the four-person crew of an interstellar warship on a multiyear mission of revenge
Through each voyager’s distinct perspective, the book explores artificial intelligence, social media, and the effects of extended isolation
One character doesn’t care about these aliens’ civilization; he is content just to kill as many as possible
Another is driven to discover more; a third is focused on maintaining the morale of the others, even as she herself unravels
And their captain has to balance their individual needs against the requirements of the mission
Barry provides riveting, rewarding action without sacrificing smarts or character development
This quick read explores mankind’s dueling urges to connect and destroy, our divergent responses to the unknown, and how far some among us will go to protect ourselves and the people we care about

Organized by the 23-year-old pop star Olivia Rodrigo, the inaugural edition of the festival featured an all-female lineup and raised $20 million—half of which was donated by Melinda French Gates—for an array of women’s-rights organizations, including Planned Parenthood and the National Domestic Workers Alliance

Even as a brutal heat wave threatened to smother the energy, the fest felt like a cheerful coming-out party—an announcement of the political commitments of a generation of mainstream artists more famous for singing about the self than about society

title: The Meaning of the Lindsay Clancy Mistrial
excerpt: During the five weeks of her murder trial, Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts mother accused of murdering her three young children in 2023, spoke barely a word
body: During the five weeks of her murder trial, Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts mother accused of murdering her three young children in 2023, spoke barely a word
She has been on display for the entirety of her livestreamed trial, sitting in her wheelchair beside her lawyer at the defense table

At one point, when the prosecution walked the jury through the children’s autopsy reports, she hunched over, racked with sobs, crying out, “I can’t do this!” But mostly, Clancy has remained silent and wide-eyed, her gaze wandering around the courtroom as though searching for something
The judge in the case has just declared a mistrial because the jury has been unable to reach a unanimous verdict
But the viewing public, in the absence of Clancy’s own explanation of her experiences leading up to and after the killings, has projected its own ideas onto the case and rendered its own verdict
Some people have interpreted Clancy’s trial as a referendum on women’s postpartum mental health
Others have developed elaborate conspiracy theories maintaining that Clancy’s ex-husband, Patrick, is actually the guilty party
Still others have construed Clancy’s story as evidence for their own niche political beliefs
These are all comforting narratives, in some sense, because they imply an underlying logic that imbues the events with meaning and provides a road map for catharsis
Yet the jury’s inability to arrive at a verdict makes plain that a careful evaluation of the facts does not yield an easily intelligible conclusion
The reality may be darker and more despairing: that something so dramatic and destructive could, in the end, mean nothing at all

As Clancy’s trial has progressed, dozens of women wearing pink have appeared at organized rallies outside the courthouse in Plymouth, Massachusetts, holding signs signaling a kind of support for her. “Any one of us who have dealt with mental health, anxiety, depression, postpartum—I think we just know that any one of us could be sitting in her chair,” the organizer of a recent event billed as an opportunity to “stand in peace for Lindsay” told a local news outlet

There is something inherently unsettling about any public expression of support for a confessed killer, but these gatherings and their associated social-media movements have not seemed aimed at improving Clancy’s odds of success in court

Instead, these demonstrations suggest that Clancy has for some women become a symbolic figure : the devoted but suffering mother martyred by the relentless, punishing demands of her children’s early years and left to suffer by a flawed and fractured health-care system
Many women have felt overwhelmed to the point of drowning in the months after giving birth, and many have sought help but failed to receive it
Clancy’s case, in her supporters’ imagination, appears to be the sum of all those biological and social hazards

What happened to Clancy, in this view, was predictable, and thus preventable. [ Stephanie McCrummen: The women who are obsessed with Lindsay Clancy ] That’s a tidy narrative about what took place in Duxbury that night in 2023, when Clancy strangled her three young children to death, then attempted to end her own life by swallowing prescription drugs, slashing her neck and wrists, and then jumping out of a window

A possible upshot of this view is that it may raise awareness about the inadequacy of treatment options for postpartum mental illnesses—to the degree that raising awareness about any given issue ever meaningfully changes anything
And some elements of it seem inarguably true, such as the idea that Clancy’s psychiatric care was woefully uncoordinated
But this theory also has the odd effect of making Clancy the star of her own murder trial, for whom the viewer at home may be encouraged to root, which risks eliding the gravity of what she did
Simultaneously believing that someone is relatable and vulnerable and that they are nevertheless guilty of and accountable for heinous crimes is, however, cognitively tricky
I suspect that that tension is the origin of a similarly enormous groundswell of conspiracy theorizing about Clancy’s case that has pervaded social media

Although those theories vary, they generally maintain that Clancy is factually innocent of the killings and that her ex-husband is instead guilty of murdering the children, attempting to murder Clancy, and framing his ex-wife for the deaths

Proponents typically cite as proof any number of purported facts presented at trial, such as that Clancy’s fingerprints weren’t found on the exercise bands used to strangle the children, or that her core body temperature upon her arrival to the hospital called the prosecution’s timeline of events into question
Clancy is, in these tellings, a victim of spousal abuse akin to torture, whose partner cruelly exploited her postpartum suffering in order to dispose of his family
That, too, is a tidy story with symbolic significance: For those who deny her guilt, Clancy’s life and fate become a nightmare of female subjugation

This view morphs a reasonable claim that Patrick ought to have been more attentive to Clancy’s deteriorating mental state into a much stronger insistence that he is in fact fully culpable for what happened, having carefully plotted the entire sequence of events
Clancy’s story, then, becomes a parable about male violence against women

Yet this embrace of Clancy as the true victim of her crimes has triggered an online backlash on the political right that maintains that liberal-female support for Clancy is a naked expression of latent female tendencies toward violence against children and an indication that liberal women are unstable and dangerous. (This despite the fact that women actually have varying views on the case, and that men kill the majority of children murdered in the United States.) That thinking also mistakenly takes Clancy to be a representative Everywoman, this time standing in for the threatening volatility of liberal women writ large. [ Elizabeth Bruenig: Why Lindsay Clancy’s insanity defense might fail ] All of these views of Clancy’s case strive to make sense of her alleged crimes: This trial must mean that mothers in America are crucially underserved, or that men in America are chauvinistically exploitative, or that women in America are secretly a danger to themselves and others

Some of those readings are more compelling than others, but they all seem to overemphasize what is generalizable about the case while understating what is unique, particular, and hyper-specific about what happened
The broader the statements about this case are, the less they have to do with the events as they really occurred
Clancy’s experience was inarguably extreme
If, as the defense claims, she was suffering from postpartum psychosis, it was an ultra-rare expression of an already uncommon condition
Her psychiatric care was, per a subsequent malpractice lawsuit, allegedly mismanaged, and the severity of her purported adverse reactions to widely used medications was highly unusual

She was undoubtedly suffering in the months leading up to the murders, and it’s possible that the right degree of support could have prevented what happened, but it’s likewise true that nobody could have reasonably predicted what happened
More than any general theme or idea, Clancy’s crimes seem to have hinged on a moment of catastrophic dysfunction
Life, in the end, defies a great deal of neat storytelling
For the past several weeks, Clancy’s case has been heard in the court of public opinion

At this point, people seem desperate for answers about why these deaths happened and what they mean, or at least a guarantee that something we’ve learned from this case will prevent similar tragedies from happening in the future
Many such onlookers have hoped that the trial verdict will supply such insights

title: OpenAI Wants to Talk About The Federalist Papers
excerpt: Late last month, OpenAI launched a rather grand mission: nothing less than defending individual political freedom in an age of all-powerful machines
body: Late last month, OpenAI launched a rather grand mission: nothing less than defending individual political freedom in an age of all-powerful machines

The company’s “Strategic Futures” team has styled itself, in a sense, as inheriting the task of America’s Founding Fathers: “We labor in service of the ideals of free expression and individual liberty that are enshrined in the humble parchment of the U.S

Constitution,” Dean Ball, the team’s leader, wrote in a new OpenAI blog post. (The post opens with a quote from James Madison in The Federalist Papers .) Ball worries that advanced AI could radically concentrate power in the hands of those who control it, displacing labor in ways that disempower humans
In an extreme scenario, governments will have no need to listen to their citizens if there are robots to wage wars and omniscient software to run the bureaucracy
Ball is interested in studying what new political institutions might be needed to avoid this fate
Many Americans—a majority of whom express distrust toward the AI industry, outrage about data centers, and fears about their job security—already seem to be feeling this loss of agency very deeply
And the AI boom has already generated enormous amounts of wealth in just a handful of tech companies—including OpenAI itself
To say the least, it’s paradoxical for one of the most influential companies in the world’s most powerful industry to decry the AI-enabled concentration of power
So I reached out to Ball to understand more about his unease about the industry he works in, and how he wants to see the United States adapt to AI
Ball, who studies AI policy, is something of a minor celebrity in the industry
Last year, he joined the White House as an AI adviser and helped write the Trump administration’s AI Action Plan , a policy road map for the technology
He eventually departed, seemingly on good terms, from the administration before publicly lambasting it during its dispute with Anthropic earlier this year
Then, in July, he joined OpenAI. “My view is that we basically have transformative AI in the world now,” Ball told me. “You’re living in a world that is being transformed
It is happening.” This conversation has been edited for length and clarity
Matteo Wong: You write that concentration of power through AI could upend the basic human freedoms enshrined in the U.S
Can you elaborate on how? Dean Ball: Fundamentally, political power is the geographically bounded ability to wield the monopoly on legitimate force and violence
Doing so has heretofore required the cooperation of a great many human beings
You needed militaries, you needed people in those militaries, and you needed people to keep those militaries fed and supplied
And you needed people to pay for all of that through taxation
So people had a seat at the table because, in some sense, everything is being provided by them
Now you have to assume that robotics is going to advance soon in the same way that general digital intelligence has
But at that point, the ability to project violence no longer requires people
And it is also conceivable that AI might generate sufficient revenue that the government would not need to rely on taxing people
If you look at the politics of AI, I think Americans are smart and have a sense that their seat at the table might be getting smaller
Wong: You’re talking about concentration of power in the government, but generative AI is a technology developed in the private sector
There is potential for a rare and even unprecedented concentration of power in industry
What risks does that pose? Ball: You’re not trying to avoid all concentration of power, but to balance it
If this era gives rise to corporations that have a tremendous amount of power in the world, I think that’s good—so long as those organizations are governed
In other words, so long as the government that oversees them grows in lockstep
People tend to assume that AI residing in private hands is inherently a concentration-of-power risk

But I think that an extremely well-run, government-owned superintelligence lab is a bigger concentration-of-power risk than a polycentric world where there are many superintelligences made by different, competing companies overseen by a government
Wong: As far as private concentration of power goes, there are arguably now two frontier labs, your employer and Anthropic
The market doesn’t seem to be providing many checks on them
Ball: I think it’s a fiercely competitive market right now
And China, of course, is delivering highly capable open-source models
It’s possible this is going to commodify the products that OpenAI and Anthropic offer
I don’t agree with that, but you can’t dismiss it as a crazy outcome
OpenAI’s mission is to deliver artificial general intelligence safely to the world
If that means we’re more like a utility than we are like a big, fancy tech company, so be it
Wong: This brings us to the core of your essay

title: Why So Many Men Are Unraveling
excerpt: Jon Ronson had never really thought about the term masculinity until a strange series of events led him down a rabbit hole involving castles, cage fights, and a
body: Jon Ronson had never really thought about the term masculinity until a strange series of events led him down a rabbit hole involving castles, cage fights, and an actor playing a horse
Host Charlie Warzel talks to Ronson about the disinhibited men who are looking for purpose in all the wrong places

Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube The following is a transcript of the episode: Jon Ronson: So I think, beginning with deindustrialization, the death of factories, office life eroding, men realizing that certain privileges they had they don’t quite have the same way anymore—feeling kind of tossed around in a sea of conflicting ideologies about what being a man actually means
Should you be more stoical? Should you be more vulnerable? You know, all of these men’s-health influencers giving these differing, contrasting ideas
And so this is a huge societal shift in many different ways
You’ve got men responding to these changes by bowing out, and then you’ve got these other men who are responding by spiraling

Charlie Warzel: I’m Charlie Warzel, and this is Galaxy Brain , and today we are headed down a rabbit hole that includes ominous castles, public shaming, YouTube, White House cage fighting, all to answer one of life’s burning questions

Why is it that so many men are unraveling these days? Is this part of a changing economy? Part of a bad job market? Is it fallout from the pandemic? Or, is it part of something bigger? A societal failure of some sort, or an outgrowth of what some people have called the masculinity crisis? Now those words, masculinity crisis , can cause some people to roll their eyes
Men, of course, continue to enjoy all kinds of societal privilege, and gender inequities abound

But what is clear, I think, if you spent any time engaging with modern politics and culture, is that over the last few decades there has been a very real, if hard to define, debate over what it means to be a man
Jobs and gender roles—they’ve changed, and culture along with it
But that change has also created some uncertainty for the men who have been used to being at the center of every household, every office, every institution, marketing campaign, and political decision

And it’s in that uncertainty that all kinds of voices, pickup artists, politicians, incels on 4chan, Andrew Tate, Jordan Peterson—you name it—they’ve all jumped in to offer these competing visions of masculinity
Now, some of this has taken the form of toxic, misogynistic, manosphere bullshit
Some of it is just positive or harmless—“dudes rock” kind of stuff
And so many of these lessons, they end up being taught or absorbed, for better or for worse, in online communities and communicated by people who may or may not have ulterior motives
So what happens to regular men in this bizarre online stew that we’re all in? My guest today, the writer and podcaster Jon Ronson, explores that in his new book, The Castle
Ronson, to be clear, isn’t really writing about the manosphere or the high-profile grifters or the wild extremes
Instead, Ronson focuses on ordinary people who tend to find themselves in extraordinary situations
For the past three years, Ronson has been reporting on what happens to men when institutions die, when technology lets a million influencers bloom, and culture changes rapidly
What I find so useful about Ronson’s work is that it is curious and is funny, but it’s not overly ideological
The Castle is written partly as a mystery and partly as a work of anthropology
For the last decade, Ronson and I have crossed paths on stories numerous times
Like me, his work is always trying to understand what pushes people to believe strange or awful things, and all the ways that technology warps culture, which in turn warps real human beings
So—are men okay? Has the internet driven us all insane? It turns out this is a very complicated question
And Jon Ronson joins me now to talk about it all
Warzel: Jon Ronson, welcome to Galaxy Brain
Ronson: Charlie, it’s a delight to be here
Warzel: So your newest book, the reason you are talking to me right now—it’s called The Castle , and you’ve written it in such a propulsive, narrative way
But the story is also unique, I think, in that it found you
So tell me a bit about the castle and how it entered your life in what is clearly an extremely personal way
I am asleep, and I wake up, and there’s a series of texts from my son, who was in his mid-20s at the time
And so I read the last text first, and the last text says something like: It’s okay; that was completely fucked, but we got out, and we’re safe now
Ronson: So I frantically read the other texts
And what I gather is that him and three friends have been invited to a party being held by a stranger that one of them had met on Tinder
So it’s like three hours’ drive outside of New York City, into the Connecticut countryside
And when they turn up, this man’s house is a vast, newly built Gothic castle, which is ostentatious even by Gothic-castle standards
And so they tentatively cross the drawbridge over the moat and enter to discover that there is no party
They’ve been lured there for some mysterious other reason

So the castle owner comes out, and they say, “I’m sorry, but where’s the party?” And he said, “No, I’ve invited you here to take part in my reality show.” So they said, “What’s the name of your reality show?” And he said, “It’s called 101 Princesses .” They asked what the core concept of 101 Princesses was, and he said, “I’m the lord

title: A Movie Can’t Be Just Its Own Thing Anymore
excerpt: Onslaught , in theaters this week, should be the perfect early-September treat
body: Onslaught , in theaters this week, should be the perfect early-September treat

The aggressive action thriller is gory, loud, and packed with interesting actors, and it has a straightforward premise: Three murderous super-soldiers, the result of some shadowy extra-governmental experiment, have escaped from a lab and are descending upon a small town in New Mexico

A tough-as-nails retired Army sniper named Celeste (played by Adria Arjona), living somewhat off the grid in a trailer park, must use her grit and know-how to defend herself against the oncoming attack
Yet as simple as that sounds, the film feels needlessly complex
Rather than just delivering on its clean setup, it becomes fixated on teasing future installments—a symptom of the obsession with sequelization that’s affecting even smaller genre films
The director Adam Wingard was, once upon a time, a master of the cheap thrill

This is a compliment; he emerged from the micro-budget mumblecore scene in the 2000s, then made two impressively nasty bits of horror—the slasher You’re Next and the wonderfully tawdry and tense The Guest
But Wingard has spent years trapped in franchise drudgery, offering up an unnecessary follow-up to The Blair Witch Project and a pair of giant-scale, instantly forgettable Godzilla movies
Onslaught initially suggests a more back-to-basics turn for the director, a return to R-rated indies that are unencumbered by cinematic universes
That mission, however, seems to have been a little corrupted by what Wingard’s been working on in the meantime

Its aesthetics are top-notch, the opening credits unfolding as an invigorating blitz of conspiratorial imagery that cuts together cable-news clips of several presidents, including Richard Nixon, Bill Clinton, and George W
Bush, with drone footage of overseas combat; the entire sequence feels like a fever dream of the early 2000s
Celeste is a veteran of an unspecified overseas combat engagement, and the audience briefly glimpses in flashback the traumatic firefights that preceded her discharge
Living alongside her in the desert trailer park is a crew of other misfits, including the bumbling policeman Kovacks (Eric Wareheim) and a cantankerous older fella named Josiah (Reginald VelJohnson)

To Celeste’s annoyance, her ex-husband drops off their cherubic daughter that day to stay the weekend; the tension is, of course, quickly building to a violent incursion. [ Read: Hollywood’s star power is shifting ] Part of my irritation with the film, though, stems from just how jazzed I felt about its first act
The actor Dan Stevens, at this point a longtime collaborator of Wingard’s (including, most recently, the director’s previous Godzilla movie), dons nightmarish makeup to play Dr
Hans Kammler; he’s a German-speaking mad scientist in charge of the military experiment that goes wrong
Rebecca Hall, another Godzilla alum, is Dr
Kammler’s domineering wife, Hanna—a stiletto-clad, cigarette-smoking badass boasting some mysteriously derived authority

The duo’s cartoonish poise is a delight to witness, as is their ridiculous hubris: Whatever lab simulation they’ve designed for their seemingly zombified super-soldiers quickly falls apart, leading the latter to invade the surrounding environs

Some solid gunplay follows, and the final showdown between Celeste and her trailer-park buds and the soldiers has some brutal flourishes—though it irritatingly takes place at night, making the chaos a little harder to see
But the screenplay (written by Simon Barrett) teases revelations throughout, then delivers on practically none of them
Kammler’s work remains nebulous, and Celeste’s backstory is only vaguely filled in
These gaps would be forgivable if Onslaught existed mostly to deliver the frivolity that Wingard once excelled at; instead, it ends on a cliff-hanger that hints at further developments
In interviews, the director has even alluded to the movie belonging to a growing shared universe alongside You’re Next and The Guest , though there’s no real on-screen evidence of that
I am not opposed to Wingard building connections among his works, especially if he’s looking to do it in a more intentional way
Too often, though, Onslaught acts like it’s making moves in that direction without a real sense of purpose

The Godzilla -centric enterprise that Wingard has spent the past few years in, also known as the “Monsterverse,” relies on the kind of lazy storytelling that films designed to spawn numerous sequels tend to tell: Rather than ending punchily, the movie lands on a big conflict that sets up new villains and crossover possibilities
Perhaps Onslaught will be a big enough hit to get a similar treatment, even on a smaller scale
More likely, though, the lack of resolution will leave people feeling as dissatisfied as I did.

title: Architecting memory and storage in the AI era
excerpt: Imagine a healthcare system analyzing millions of data points in real time to accelerate life-saving medical research, or an intelligent assistant instantly res
body: Imagine a healthcare system analyzing millions of data points in real time to accelerate life-saving medical research, or an intelligent assistant instantly resolving thousands of complex customer needs at once

These real-world breakthroughs rely on advanced infrastructure acting as the engine of continuous intelligence, powering real-time services while also supporting an increasingly intelligent edge of IoT and consumer devices
However, in this inference-driven landscape, every delay, bottleneck, or wasted watt directly affects human outcomes and operating costs.  This shift changes what infrastructure must deliver
Performance, latency, memory bandwidth, storage throughput, and networking cannot be optimized in silos

Inference workloads are continuous, geographically distributed, and highly sensitive to response time, requiring systems designed for scale, resilience, and efficiency from the start. “We tend to think of AI as a single workload, and it’s not
It’s thousands, it’s millions, it’s billions of different workloads,” says Jim McGregor, founder and principal analyst, Tirias Research
AI inference changes the optimization problem from one of raw compute to coordinated infrastructure—memory, storage, and networking
For business leaders, the priority is clear: AI infrastructure decisions must balance cost, flexibility, and future readiness
The winners will be organizations that improve performance per watt, reduce environmental footprint, and remove memory and storage bottlenecks before they limit growth
AI inference requires a new architectural approach Systems for AI need to be rearchitected because shoehorning modern AI systems into legacy infrastructure limits AI’s transformative potential
Purpose-built architectures are essential to realize the true value of AI, from accelerating scientific discovery to creating truly autonomous digital agents

Traditional enterprise IT has been able to rely on relatively stable infrastructure assumptions, but inference and agentic AI introduce new demands around latency, data movement, scalability, and utilization that make architecture choices far more consequential. “Data centers must now support continuous, distributed, and increasingly real-time AI services—none of which are a single workload,” says McGregor. “They all require different requirements from a system-level perspective.” To support real-time AI, enterprises can no longer view memory and storage merely as supporting hardware, but at the heart of the system
Organizations need to architect a data pipeline that can rapidly ingest, clean, transform, store, move, and deliver data

Inference workloads place sustained pressure on infrastructure in ways that look very different from earlier training-centric deployments, demanding continuous data retrieval and caching that traditional applications never required
Accordingly, performance by itself is no longer the sole benchmark that matters

Enterprises increasingly must balance performance with efficiency, cost, and scalability, especially as they try to support different AI services without overbuilding infrastructure for peak conditions. “You have to optimize the entire network, and that includes memory and storage, around the types of workloads you plan on running,” says McGregor. “You have to really have a detailed understanding of what those workloads are going to be.” Any AI infrastructure strategy must start with workload awareness
Inference, agentic AI, and other emerging AI use cases require organizations to treat the data center as an integrated system

Data movement is the new bottleneck and an opportunity for competitive advantage As enterprises deploy advanced inference and agentic systems, the sheer volume of data being queried in real time has made data movement the most pressing constraint
Modern AI techniques like retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) require systems to constantly scan massive databases to generate accurate responses
This requires immense computing power, but more importantly, it requires immediate access to data

McGregor says the focus shift to how efficiently data can be moved, cached, and delivered across the broader architecture elevates memory and storage from background infrastructure to strategic assets. “The biggest thing we’re doing right now is moving data from one place to another and making sure that we can use it effectively.” Because AI is not a single workload category, simply buying the fastest processors is insufficient
Inference depends heavily on memory bandwidth, caching, storage proximity, and the ability to retrieve relevant information quickly and consistently
Understanding where each resource belongs in the stack and how those layers interact under real operating conditions has become a business imperative

The most effective AI infrastructure looks less like a collection of best-in-class parts and more like a balanced system of compute, memory, storage, and networking, McGregor says, because bottlenecks tend to migrate from one layer to the next. “You have to architect all four together to be efficient, and that’s the challenge.” The interdependence of data-plane design and network bandwidth means AI infrastructure planning has become a business decision just as much as an engineering one: latency is now inseparable from value
In robotics, financial services, healthcare, and customer-facing AI systems, delays are not merely technical imperfections; they can undermine safety, responsiveness, or trust
AI infrastructure performance becomes a matter of reputation management

The organizations that gain the most from AI may not be those with the largest clusters, but those with the clearest understanding of how to align every infrastructure element to effectively execute AI workloads
Building an AI infrastructure procurement framework Planning AI infrastructure is not simply about choosing the fastest hardware

It is about how to scale without locking the organization into assumptions that may quickly become obsolete. “You need to be flexible because the demands are going to change rapidly and the technology is changing rapidly,” McGregor says
Future-proofing AI infrastructure requires keeping your options open as workloads, economics, and architectures keep shifting: Define the AI workloads that are being optimized
Infrastructure choices must match business needs rather than what McGregor calls generic “AI readiness,” which risks overspending in some areas while leaving bottlenecks unresolved in others
Build a modular architecture for compute, memory, storage, power, and cooling so capacity can change as demand shifts rather than committing too early to a rigid architecture
Work with the full ecosystem of suppliers and integrators to reduce supply risk and improve access to the right components
McGregor says buyers can no longer assume their OEM or cloud provider alone will insulate them from supply constraints or architectural complexity
Reassess your procurement strategy continuously
AI requirements, hardware, and business models are changing too quickly for a fixed long-term design
Optimize for efficiency and ROI, not just peak performance
The most powerful setup may be too costly to sustain
Efficiency is also a public-facing metric—better utilization and more workload-aware system design can help companies respond to growing scrutiny around power consumption and water use
The strategic goal of smarter AI data center design is not maximum performance at any cost, but an adaptable architecture that can deliver value, absorb change, and justify its footprint

title: Data from drones in Ukraine is fueling a new Wild West marketplace
excerpt: Battlefields in Ukraine are littered with the remnants of drones, which are now firmly established as a critical weapon of modern warfare
body: Battlefields in Ukraine are littered with the remnants of drones, which are now firmly established as a critical weapon of modern warfare
But behind all that wreckage, there’s a new gold mine for the defense sector

The data drones generate will far outlast the wars in which they are used to fight, increasingly becoming part of the AI architecture that shapes even civilian life.   For every flight, unmanned systems collect thousands of points of data, from images and video to controller inputs
Together, those records show how a machine and a person responded to constantly shifting circumstances.  Ukraine has now begun converting that experience into a resource

Its Ministry of Defense announced in January that it would make millions of data points gathered during tens of thousands of drone flights available to both military contractors and commercial companies, and since then more than 100 companies and the UK government have gained access
For a country at war, it’s a quick way to attract funding and partnerships
But this step turns the front line into an active site of model training, taking advantage of how the chaos of war creates conditions that AI companies struggle to reproduce on their own
Other countries and battlefields are likely to follow Ukraine’s lead, but the responsibility for governing this new industry cannot fall solely on a country fighting for its survival

That legal vacuum has to be filled together by the countries and companies involved in this industry’s development.   Explosive growth Ukraine’s battlefields are not the first to produce records used to train and develop models: American drones over Syria and Yemen collected data that informed the first generation of semiautonomous military hardware in the late 2010s
The difference now is that access to that data is being used to develop a wider ecosystem
And the financial value to defense firms is immense: Battlefield data offers large volumes of machine experience gathered under conditions that no laboratory can produce
That’s because the data that’s most valuable for training AI models comes from exceptions: the moment visibility disappears, a signal jams, or a human operator improvises
AI companies spend years and enormous sums trying to capture enough of these moments to make their models more robust
But war produces them at a frequency controlled testing cannot match
This constantly changing terrain is what makes drone data valuable far beyond the battlefield
A commercial drone used for delivery or remote sensing may never encounter artillery fire, but it must still operate with incomplete information in a world where people behave unpredictably
The same problem is compressed by war into a much shorter timeline.  Processed and matched against records of what its operator was doing, that data turns operational records into training sets
Many conflicts have already seen this training loop happen as drone footage feeds subsequent generations of military technology, and the market is set to grow

Enabled Intelligence, an American company that specializes in processing data to become usable in AI training, says it has already made more than half a million hours of Ukrainian drone footage available to feed into the next round of models, advertising possible uses in both military and commercial systems
Closing the data loop Many of the drones that now define our modern age of warfare began as civilian technology

But they’ve recently been turbocharged by new, commercially available AI systems, which allow cheap machines to operate autonomously—either individually or as a flock—as the environment changes around them
Each flight then creates a record of what the system encountered
The controlled lab environments usually developed to train these autonomous systems can approximate failure but are no match for  the live conditions of a battlefield with very real risks

Military intelligence programs have held data generated by sensor-heavy systems like Predator and Reaper drones for nearly a decade through programs like Project Maven, but access remained entirely within the defense world

The data generated was available only through restricted, classified channels for the sole purpose of developing new weapons systems that would feed back into the same military that produced the data in the first place
That experience is now being shared to a much broader development network.  The loop now closes

Commercial technologies adapted for the battlefield are generating data that can flow back into the industries from which they came, becoming part of the data infrastructure relied on by governments and the private sector alike.  Drones that were trained in the signal-jammed airspace over Ukraine are now being deployed in the agricultural sector to help farmers map and survey their fields in places lacking the cell signal necessary for previous generations of technology.  Other countries are likely to follow Ukraine in selling their battlefield data, and we are not ready for the new marketplace this will create
Bad actors could acquire the data, but purchase controls already mitigate that risk
Intelligence operatives scrutinize potential customers’ infrastructure for ways that data could reach enemies or nefarious actors.  Training data creates a new tracing problem, though

Whereas the movement of commercial datasets can be followed when planted contact details appear two steps from the original buyer, the provenance of AI training data vanishes in a manner embedded in the technology itself

Another risk is that this use of the data creates an extractive economy in which wealthier countries far from danger benefit from the mortal threat borne by frontline states, potentially creating a market incentive for war to continue as an unending mine for digital gold.  A fraught new frontier Existing laws regulate how militaries may conduct war

But they say almost nothing about what happens when records created in combat are stripped of their operational context, packaged as data, and licensed to companies whose products circulate far beyond where they were made
The responsibilities of the companies that design these systems remain unsettled

Ukraine is building access controls, which are mentioned in the newly signed UK-Ukraine AI agreement, but no governments are actively working on regulating what happens when data has been absorbed into a model and crosses back into civilian markets
The soldiers and civilians visible in them did not agree to become training material for products that might be sold years later
But sensor data, camera footage, and coordinates from civilians fleeing a drone strike now constitute the sorts of data that inform how future machines will make decisions
Individuals featured in the data—be they targets, controllers, or civilians standing by—become part of the training material
The autonomous capabilities based on that data do not stop at the edge of the battlefield
Such capabilities move into other military or commercial systems like delivery vehicles or agricultural machinery
Errors and assumptions embedded in the data travel with the model even once it enters civilian life

title: What comes next for the 1 million people who have lost – or will soon lose – Temporary Protected Status
url:
<title>What comes next for the 1 million people who have lost – or will soon lose – Temporary Protected Status</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757614/original/file-20260902-50-v9o6m3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C6797%2C4531&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">People hold Haitian flags and signs during a July 2026 rally in San Diego in support of immigrants living in the U.S. with Temporary Protected Status.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/Immigration%20TPS/139c819321fb441096bf602bdafda502/photo">AP Photo/Gregory Bull</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>At the beginning of President Donald Trump’s second term, <a href="https://www.americanimmigrationcouncil.org/fact-sheet/temporary-protected-status-tps-overview/">1.3 million individuals from 17 countries</a> were living and working in the U.S. under Temporary Protected Status, or TPS.</p>

<p>TPS is a humanitarian form of protection from deportation for people who cannot return to their home countries because of an armed conflict, environmental disaster or other <a href="https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/8/1254a">extraordinary circumstances</a>. </p>

<p>In 2025, the Trump administration began terminating or not renewing TPS for those countries, making its way through 13 of them. As the administration turns its attention to the few remaining nations, most TPS holders have lost or will soon lose their protection from deportation and their authorization to work. Many will be separated from their families and the communities <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2026/08/12/second-trump-administration-has-ended-temporary-protected-status-for-most-immigrants-who-had-it/">they have lived in for decades</a>. Some will be forced to return to countries like Afghanistan, Haiti and Syria, all of which are on the U.S. State Department’s <a href="https://travelmaps.state.gov/TSGMap/">“Do Not Travel” list</a> due to war, terrorism or other extreme violence. </p>

<p>As a <a href="https://gould.usc.edu/faculty/profile/jean-lantz-reisz/">law scholar</a> who studies immigration detention, I can say that most people with TPS never had a path to anything more permanent, which means, as they face deportation, they have little recourse. </p>

<h2>Challenges in court</h2>

<p>In the fall of 2025, the Trump White House announced that it would not renew Syrian or Haitian TPS; Syria’s would expire in 60 days, Haiti’s in February 2026. Lower courts blocked both terminations, triggering appeals that took the cases to the Supreme Court.</p>

<p>In June 2026, in Mullin v. Doe, <a href="https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/25pdf/25-1083_f204.pdf">the Supreme Court ruled</a> that federal courts cannot review most challenges to a TPS termination because, in <a href="https://guides.loc.gov/latinx-civil-rights/tps">the original 1990 law creating TPS</a>, Congress barred judicial review of the decision to give a country TPS – or extend or end it.</p>

<p>James Percival, the general counsel of the Department of Homeland Security, <a href="https://www.dhs.gov/news/2026/06/25/dhs-issues-statement-following-multiple-supreme-court-wins">celebrated the decision</a>, saying “Temporary Protected Status was always supposed to be temporary and can be canceled at the appropriate time.”</p>

<p>But the ruling means no court can consider whether a cancellation is, in fact, “appropriate,” or whether it follows the law. </p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="A young person at a rally holds a sign that reads 'families deserve to stay together in the place they call home.'" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757616/original/file-20260902-50-mk112x.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757616/original/file-20260902-50-mk112x.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757616/original/file-20260902-50-mk112x.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757616/original/file-20260902-50-mk112x.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757616/original/file-20260902-50-mk112x.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757616/original/file-20260902-50-mk112x.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757616/original/file-20260902-50-mk112x.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">A local student holds a sign in support of Temporary Protected Status in Miami’s Little Haiti neighborhood in January 2026.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/Haiti%20Vigil%20Miami/af42e2a7695e4c9aafaf1d75de9dac88/photo">AP Photo/Lynne Sladky</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Unanswered questions</h2>

<p>When Congress passed TPS as part of <a href="https://www.congress.gov/bill/101st-congress/senate-bill/358">the Immigration Act of 1990</a>, it was responding to a specific failure: the ad hoc and inconsistent use of something called Extended Voluntary Departure, which permitted a noncitizen to remain in the U.S. <a href="https://www.supremecourt.gov/DocketPDF/25/25-1083/404231/20260413110419518_MiotCongress_Amici%20Document%20%20%20%20%20April%2013%202026%20EFile.pdf">regardless of their immigration status</a>. </p>

<p>That discretionary relief allowed some displaced Salvadorans to remain in the U.S. during their country’s civil war in the 1980s, but its application was arbitrary and often <a href="https://ccrjustice.org/home/what-we-do/our-cases/american-baptist-churches-v-thornburgh">discriminatory</a>. Because the <a href="https://americanarchive.org/exhibits/newshour-cold-war/el-salvador">U.S. backed the Salvadoran government</a>, Salvadorans were denied both Extended Voluntary Departure and asylum <a href="https://www.migrationpolicy.org/journal/country-profile/el-salvador-despite-end-civil-war-emigration-continues">more than 90% of the time</a> – not for lack of merit but because of the government they were fleeing.   </p>

<p>Congress recognized a humanitarian need for more uniform protection for people who, like Salvadorans, faced a return to violence or extreme danger but were not covered by narrow asylum laws that require proof of targeted persecution. </p>

<p>A new protected status would “standardize the procedure for granting temporary stays of deportation,” <a href="https://www.supremecourt.gov/DocketPDF/25/25-1083/404231/20260413110419518_MiotCongress_Amici%20Document%20%20%20%20%20April%2013%202026%20EFile.pdf">Representative Sander Levin explained</a> at the time.</p>

<p>“Refugees, spawned by the sad and tragic forces of warfare, should not be subject to the vagaries of our domestic politics as well,” Levin added. When the 1990 Immigration Act passed, El Salvador was the first country designated for TPS.</p>

<p>Congress avoided placing time limits on these new TPS designations, leaving that to the discretion of the presidential administration, which would evaluate a country’s humanitarian needs <a href="https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/RS20844">at least every 18 months</a>. Whether TPS holders should ever gain something more permanent was left for future congressional action.</p>

<h2>No next step</h2>

<p>Not every person from a TPS-designated country is eligible for it. Anything that disqualifies someone from asylum – national security concerns, persecuting others or criminal history – also <a href="https://www.uscis.gov/humanitarian/temporary-protected-status">disqualifies them from TPS</a>. </p>

<p>Congress did not want to incentivize unlawful immigration. For that reason, it wrote the law in such a way that TPS itself could not lead to permanent residence. Lawful permanent residents are eligible to become citizens <a href="https://www.uscis.gov/citizenship/learn-about-citizenship/citizenship-and-naturalization/i-am-a-lawful-permanent-resident-of-5-years">after five years</a>. TPS recipients, though living in the U.S. lawfully, are not classified as lawful permanent residents. </p>

<p>Congress has since passed laws creating a pathway to permanent residence for certain nationalities, including some with TPS – the <a href="https://www.uscis.gov/humanitarian/refugees-and-asylum/asylum/nicaraguan-adjustment-and-central-american-relief-act-nacara-203-eligibility-to-apply-with-uscis">Nicaraguan Adjustment and Central American Relief Act</a>, for example. It did not do so for most.</p>

<p>TPS designations for some countries have ended after a few years, like Rwanda and Guinea; others have been renewed for decades, like El Salvador, Honduras and Nicaragua. Over the years, TPS became a kind of limbo status, dependent on each presidential administration’s regular evaluation of a country’s humanitarian conditions – and on Congress to turn TPS into a pathway to lawful permanent residence. For most, the latter never happened. </p>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>What happens when TPS ends?</h2>

<p>Many people who lose TPS are not eligible for any other immigration status. </p>

<p><a href="https://www.uscis.gov/green-card/green-card-processes-and-procedures/adjustment-of-status">Lawful permanent residence</a>, commonly known as a “green card,” is mainly available in three ways: through a close family relationship, like being married to a U.S. citizen or lawful permanent resident; through a job that requires special skills, like being a professional soccer player; or through asylum status. </p>

<p>Even if a person can apply for permanent residence, their immigration history, such as entering the U.S. without a visa or remaining in the U.S. without lawful status for a certain time, <a href="https://www.scotusblog.com/cases/sanchez-v-mayorkas/">may be a permanent barrier</a>. </p>

<p>TPS holders are given at least <a href="https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/8/1254a">60 days’ notice</a> before termination takes effect, at which point they lose authorization to work and become undocumented, meaning they can be arrested by immigration officers at any time. There is little they can do in those 60 days that would allow them to lawfully remain in the U.S.</p>

<p>A TPS holder who has been continuously present in the U.S. for more than two years has a right to an immigration hearing before removal, where they may be able to apply for asylum or other relief. Others may hope to switch to a different status, but most TPS holders cannot obtain a student or employment visa. Some would have to apply from outside the U.S., some face years of quota backlogs, and some are from countries under a travel ban.</p>

<p>Past immigration violations or insufficient financial resources would also disqualify them. Most significantly, TPS holders are unlikely to convince an immigration officer that they intend to return home after their visa’s purpose is complete, as most visas require – especially someone from a country in distress due to violence or environmental disaster, the reason they have TPS in the first place. </p>

<p>Some <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2026/08/12/second-trump-administration-has-ended-temporary-protected-status-for-most-immigrants-who-had-it/">300,000 people</a> from El Salvador, Sudan, Ukraine and Lebanon are set to lose status this year. <a href="https://travel.state.gov/content/travel/en/international-travel/International-Travel-Country-Information-Pages/Ukraine.html">Ukraine</a> and <a href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/08/06/middleeast/americans-lebanon-homes-destroyed-israel-latam-intl">Lebanon</a> are in active war, so terminating TPS means deporting those people to war zones, which is what TPS was meant to prevent. Some TPS holders from El Salvador and Sudan have lived in the U.S. for more than 20 years. </p>

<p>Perhaps the 1990 Congress did not anticipate that individuals with TPS would make the U.S. their home for so long. Whatever it envisioned, it did not limit TPS to a fixed time. In my analysis, Percival’s assertion that TPS was always meant to be temporary is not, by itself, an “appropriate” reason to end protection. </p>

<p>As <a href="https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/25pdf/25-1083_f204.pdf">Justice Elena Kagan stated in her dissent</a> to the recent Supreme Court ruling, even if TPS does not promise “never-ending humanitarian protection,” the end of it for certain individuals – like the plaintiffs in Mullin v. Doe – could deliver them to “devastating, and indeed life-threatening, injury.”</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/290292/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

In 2025, the Trump administration began terminating or not renewing TPS for those countries, making its way through 13 of them

Many will be separated from their families and the communities they have lived in for decades

State Department’s “Do Not Travel” list due to war, terrorism or other extreme violence

<title>Farmer-poet Wendell Berry’s environmental ethics were deeply rooted in his Christian faith and belief in caring for creation</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757904/original/file-20260903-50-9xbk1d.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C66%2C4332%2C2888&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Wendell Berry, right, joins an &#39;I Love Mountains&#39; rally against mountaintop mining at the Kentucky Capitol in 2013. </span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/KY%20Mountaintop%20Removal/244ed389603d4cb6a684afa6402885f0/photo">AP Photo/James Crisp</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>For most of his 92 years, Wendell Berry farmed his Lane’s Landing homestead in Henry County, Kentucky, using <a href="https://www.counterpointpress.com/books/the-unsettling-of-america/">methods that embraced the land</a>. He preferred draft horses to diesel-powered tractors and used crop rotation and manure fertilizer to naturally nurture his fields.</p>

<p>The <a href="https://religionnews.com/2026/09/01/wendell-berry-writer-and-farmer-extolled-by-many-as-a-modern-day-prophet-dies-at-92/">widely revered</a> poet-farmer, who wrote passionately about rural American life and humans’ responsibility to care for the land, believed in practicing what he preached.</p>

<p>Those beliefs were rooted firmly in <a href="https://www.christianitytoday.com/2026/09/wendell-berry-obituary-novelist-poet-christian-agriculture/">his Christian Baptist faith</a>.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/95VcefsgsfE?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">Wendell Berry interviewed by Bill Moyers. The Berry Center.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Throughout his life, Berry, who died on Aug. 31, 2026, was a leading <a href="https://www.loa.org/books/606-what-i-stand-on-the-collected-essays-of-wendell-berry-1969-2017-boxed-set/">advocate of environmental stewardship</a>. You might recognize his belief system in what’s known as <a href="https://biologos.org/common-questions/why-should-christians-care-for-creation">creation care</a> today. </p>

<p>It embraces a responsibility to care for the Earth and all its creatures. Berry increasingly saw that ethic violated by the industrialization of agriculture and ignored by a <a href="https://www.christiancentury.org/article/features/quiet-rise-christian-dominionism">dominionist theology</a>, preached by some prominent American Christians, which holds that humans have a God-given right to exploit the Earth’s resources.</p>

<h2>Biblical base for Berry’s environmental ethics</h2>

<p>Berry’s environmental ethics had their basis in Genesis, the first book of the Bible, which emphasizes that humans are not the owners of the Earth but rather are called to be caregivers and to tend the planet. He wrote, “We are allowed to make no exceptions – every person’s obligation toward creation is <a href="https://www.christiancentury.org/article/2004-11/hymn-creation">summed up in two words from Genesis 2:15</a>: ‘Keep it.’” </p>

<p>In contrast, the <a href="https://www.christiancentury.org/article/features/quiet-rise-christian-dominionism">dominionist view emphasizes</a> Genesis 1:8, which has been interpreted by some to mean that humans are to subdue the Earth and to establish Christian dominance. </p>

<p>Berry opposed the idea that Christian scripture advocated for environmentally destructive practices such as mountaintop-removal coal mining, which led to the destruction of streams and forests in his native Kentucky. In 2011, he participated in a multiday sit-in protest of the mining practices, saying, “I <a href="https://sojo.net/articles/wendell-berry-wont-quit-trying-save-mountains">intend to stay interested in it and involved</a> as long as the Lord spares me.” </p>



<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757853/original/file-20260903-60-lfn7qb.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="An image from a social media site" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757853/original/file-20260903-60-lfn7qb.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757853/original/file-20260903-60-lfn7qb.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=340&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757853/original/file-20260903-60-lfn7qb.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=340&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757853/original/file-20260903-60-lfn7qb.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=340&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757853/original/file-20260903-60-lfn7qb.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=428&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757853/original/file-20260903-60-lfn7qb.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=428&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757853/original/file-20260903-60-lfn7qb.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=428&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Wendell Berry, who died on Aug. 31, 2026, shared some thoughts on Instagram in 2024.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.instagram.com/p/DBFI6IRSALp/">WendellBerryPoems/Instagram</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>I am a <a href="https://history.uiowa.edu/people/kristy-nabhan-warren">scholar of American Christianity</a> and have spent my career researching and writing about how Christians practice their beliefs. I was in the audience when Berry was awarded the 2013 American Academy of Religion’s <a href="https://aarweb.org/award/martin-e-marty-award-for-the-public-understanding-of-religion/">Martin Marty honor for the Public Understanding of Religion</a>. For over an hour I listened raptly, as did the rest of the standing-room-only crowd, as he detailed his love for the land, community and his wife, Tanya.</p>

<p>I also taught students using his book “<a href="https://www.counterpointpress.com/books/jayber-crow/">Jayber Crow</a>,” about small-town living, religion and community, in my honors course at a small liberal arts college in the Midwest. I returned to his work when I was researching modern-day agriculture in Iowa for my book “<a href="https://uncpress.org/9781469663494/meatpacking-america/">Meatpacking America</a>”.  </p>

<figure class="align-right zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757851/original/file-20260903-50-k89nnt.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A book cover with a farmer in a field" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757851/original/file-20260903-50-k89nnt.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=237&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757851/original/file-20260903-50-k89nnt.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=709&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757851/original/file-20260903-50-k89nnt.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=709&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757851/original/file-20260903-50-k89nnt.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=709&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757851/original/file-20260903-50-k89nnt.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=891&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757851/original/file-20260903-50-k89nnt.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=891&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757851/original/file-20260903-50-k89nnt.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=891&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">A photo of Wendell Berry on his farm graces the cover of a set of his books. The title captures his respect for the land.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/600044/what-i-stand-on-the-collected-essays-of-wendell-berry-1969-2017-by-wendell-berry/">Penguin Random House</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>I saw how Berry’s beliefs that humans have a responsibility to care for the Earth shaped his critiques about “agripower,” which he viewed as <a href="https://www.counterpointpress.com/books/the-unsettling-of-america-50th-anniversary-edition/">showing little regard for the fertility of the soil</a> or the “health, wisdom, thrift, or stewardship of the farming community.” His poems, fiction and nonfiction often <a href="https://www.loa.org/books/606-what-i-stand-on-the-collected-essays-of-wendell-berry-1969-2017-boxed-set/">advocated for consuming less and living more communally</a>.</p>

<p>Those beliefs rested on his <a href="https://www.counterpointpress.com/books/the-unsettling-of-america/">commitment to caring for God’s creation</a>.</p>

<h2>The idea of ‘enough’</h2>

<p>Berry’s <a href="https://www.counterpointpress.com/books/the-long-legged-house/">Christianity-infused agrarianism</a> began in earnest in the 1970s and helped popularize family-run farms, organic farming and farm-to-table eating establishments.</p>

<p>The modern creation care movement began as part of a wider network of American social justice movements. It took shape in the 1980s and ’90s, especially <a href="https://denverseminary.edu/2023/06/13/evangelicals-and-creation-care/">among those Christian evangelicals</a> who read the Book of Genesis as instructing humans to care about all of God’s creations. Today, creation care is a <a href="https://oikoumene.org/news/christians-are-called-to-care-for-creation">broad Christian movement</a> that calls for environmental stewardship, repairing the harm that humans have done to the environment, and belief in a loving God who is responsible for the Earth’s creation.</p>

<p>As the religious studies scholar <a href="https://users.drew.edu/lkearns/about.html">Laurel Kerns</a> has written, the Christian environmental movement that began in the 1980s laid the theological groundwork for creation care. Today’s many chapters of creation care form <a href="https://doi.org/10.2307/3712004">part of a religious environmental movement</a> that calls for Christians to embrace stewardship, creation spirituality and ecojustice. </p>

<p>As he detailed his 1977 text “<a href="https://www.counterpointpress.com/books/the-unsettling-of-america-50th-anniversary-edition/">The Unsettling of America</a>,” Berry was a fierce critic of agribusiness and <a href="https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/667717/why-i-am-not-going-to-buy-a-computer-by-wendell-berry/">American’s throwaway, consumeristic culture</a>. He admired the Amish lifestyle, which forgoes modern conveniences for simple farm living focused on God and family. He wrote, “It is possible, I think, to say that this is a Christian agriculture, formed upon the understanding that it is sinful for people to misuse or destroy what they did not make. The Creation is a unique, irreplaceable gift, therefore <a href="https://www.counterpointpress.com/books/the-unsettling-of-america-50th-anniversary-edition/">to be used with humility, respect, and skill</a>.”</p>



<p>Berry encouraged people, whether or not they identified as Christian or as religious, to question technology as the Amish do, to consider its impact on the environment as well as on human lives, and to develop the concept of “enough.” He wanted people to be more intentional and reflective in their thoughts, words and actions.</p>

<p>Throughout his poems and other writing, Berry beseeched readers to focus on what they actually need and not what they want or think they need. “The <a href="https://www.counterpointpress.com/books/standing-by-words/">idea of ‘enough’</a> is alien to capitalism, which respects no limit,” he wrote.</p>

<h2>Wendell Berry’s legacy in an AI backlash</h2>

<p>Berry and his wife and collaborator for 69 years, <a href="https://www.kentuckypress.com/author/tanya-amyx-berry/">Tanya Amyx Berry</a>, built a way of life and advocated for a way of living that went against the grain of mainstream American and global culture.</p>

<p>In <a href="https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poets/wendell-berry">over 50 books and many poems</a> and talks, Berry helped lay the theological, ethical and how-to groundwork for a creation care movement that spread around the world. He consistently called out the extractive, destructive human behaviors that have posed dangers for the planet’s future.</p>

<figure class="align-center ">
